passage: Monday: Arohi tugged at the plant pot and her father, Kamal, barked, "Arohi! Stop that!" with a hard face. She froze, then wailed, not knowing what she had done. Thursday: she reached for the pot again. Kamal crouched and said quietly, "No. The pot will break." She stared at his face and let go. Sunday: her hand drifted toward the pot, then stopped. Kamal shook his head gently, and when she came over teary he held her close.

qa.q: What did Kamal say on Thursday when Arohi reached for the pot again?
qa.a: He crouched and said quietly, "No. The pot will break."

qa.q: What might Arohi have been feeling when Kamal barked at her on Monday?
qa.a: She was frightened and confused. She froze and then wailed because she did not understand what she had done.

qa.q: Why did Thursday go better than Monday, and what could Kamal keep doing?
qa.a: Kamal used a quiet, short no with the reason in a few words, so Arohi could take it in instead of panicking. Holding her close once she settled is worth keeping. 🤍

qa.q: What might Kamal have noticed on Monday that made him crouch down and speak softly later?
qa.a: He probably saw Arohi freeze and wail, which showed his hard voice scared her rather than helped her understand.

grounding: A raised voice and hard face frighten a toddler, and a short calm no with a reason plus a hug when she settles works better.

passage: Hiroshi came home tired, and his daughter Astrid, two, smacked the cat's back at the low window. "Bad girl, Astrid!" he said. She dropped her head and covered her face with both hands. Hiroshi breathed out and knelt beside her. "Sorry. You are not bad. We do not hit the cat, it hurts. You are still my Astrid, and I love you." She peeked between her fingers, then leaned into his shoulder while he showed her a soft stroke.

qa.q: Where did Astrid smack the cat?
qa.a: She smacked the cat's back at the low window.

qa.q: Why did Astrid cover her face after Hiroshi said "Bad girl"?
qa.a: She seems to feel that she herself is wrong, not just what she did. The hidden face suggests hurt and shame.

qa.q: What did Hiroshi do to repair the moment, and why does it help?
qa.a: He apologised, named the behaviour ("we do not hit the cat") and told her she is still loved, so she learns the act was wrong, not her. 🙂

qa.q: How might the cat's situation look to Astrid once Hiroshi shows her a soft stroke?
qa.a: She gets a gentler thing to do instead of hitting, and she learns that the cat can be touched kindly. It gives her a way to put things right without feeling bad about herself.

grounding: Being called bad makes a child feel she is wrong; naming the behaviour and reaffirming love repairs it.

passage: Aditi's diary, Thursday. I told my daughter Ishita, two, that the wall is not for crayons. She screamed back, threw the crayon box and hit my arm. I kept my voice low and even: "I won't let you hit. I'm here." I knelt, held her hands gently and waited while she cried. When her breathing slowed she leaned on my knee. Then I said, "Hitting hurts. Show me 'stop' with your hand." Tonight I told her father, so we can both say it the same way.

qa.q: Where was Ishita not allowed to use crayons?
qa.a: Aditi told her that the wall is not for crayons.

qa.q: What was Ishita feeling when she screamed back and hit Aditi?
qa.a: She was overwhelmed by the scolding and could not hold the feeling, which is different from being disrespectful. Her leaning on Aditi's knee afterwards shows she was looking for comfort.

qa.q: Why did Aditi wait until Ishita's breathing slowed before teaching?
qa.a: A toddler in a storm cannot take in words, so Aditi held the limit and stayed steady first. Only then did she offer the hand sign for stop.

qa.q: How might Ishita's father see the day after hearing Aditi's account?
qa.a: He may learn that Ishita was upset, not defiant, and that the limit and comfort were both given. That can help him use the same steady tone.

grounding: A toddler who screams and hits after a scolding is overwhelmed; the adult stays steady, holds the limit and calms her before teaching.

passage:
"Up! Up!" Kishore patted the tower and it wobbled.
"Kishore, you put block on block on block!" Her father, Ujjwal, clapped. "Three blocks. And you kept trying when it fell."
She squealed and grabbed another. "More!"
"Show me. How did you make it stand?"
"Da!" She set one on top, tongue out.
"Yes! Careful hands. That is a tall tower."
Kishore beamed at him, then reached for the next block.

qa.q: How many blocks did Kishore put on the tower, according to Ujjwal?
qa.a: Ujjwal said she put "block on block on block", three blocks.

qa.q: What does Kishore's reaction to the clapping suggest she feels?
qa.a: She feels proud and happy. She squeals, beams at Ujjwal and reaches for another block, so she wants to do it again.

qa.q: What makes Ujjwal's praise a good kind of praise?
qa.a: He describes what she did, stacking three blocks and trying again after it fell, and he says it warmly. That points her toward effort rather than just being told she is lovely. 😊

qa.q: What would Kishore likely take from it if Ujjwal only said "good girl" without watching?
qa.a: She might enjoy the warmth but not learn which of her actions earned it. She would have less reason to try that stacking again.

grounding: Warm, specific praise for stacking blocks and for trying again makes the child glow and repeat the effort.

passage: In the courtyard of a house at the edge of the village, Kashish took six wobbly steps from the charpai to the tulsi pot. Dadi laughed and scooped her up. "Meri rani! Jeeti raho!" She kissed her forehead, and Kashish giggled and patted Dadi's cheek. Later, Kashish reached for a biscuit before dinner. Her father Sachin said, "After roti." Dadi nodded. "Haan, roti pehle." After a small grumble, Kashish crawled to her plate.

qa.q: How many steps did Kashish take before she reached the tulsi pot?
qa.a: She took six wobbly steps from the charpai to the tulsi pot.

qa.q: How can you tell Kashish feels special and safe with Dadi?
qa.a: She giggles and pats Dadi's cheek after the blessing and hug, and she is easy and playful in Dadi's arms.

qa.q: Why did it matter that Dadi agreed with Sachin about the biscuit?
qa.a: When both adults say roti first, Kashish gets the same rule from each, so the routine stays clear even though Dadi is so loving. 😊

qa.q: How might Sachin feel watching his mother celebrate Kashish's steps?
qa.a: He is probably glad that Kashish is so cherished, and Dadi backing his rule shows they are on the same side.

grounding: A grandmother's blessing and hug after a small achievement makes the child feel special, while the adults keep the same rules.

passage: Monday: Naveen sat on the sofa with his phone. Farhan brought a toy car and tugged his sleeve. "Papa, Papa!" No answer, so Farhan cried louder. Thursday: Farhan sat by the table with the car and did not look up when Naveen came in. Saturday: after tea Naveen put the phone in a drawer and sat on the floor. Farhan watched his face for a while, then slowly pushed the car across the floor to him.

qa.q: What did Farhan do on Monday to get Naveen's attention?
qa.a: He brought a toy car, tugged Naveen's sleeve, called "Papa, Papa!" and then cried louder.

qa.q: What might Farhan's silence on Thursday mean about how he feels?
qa.a: After louder crying did not work, he seems to have stopped trying to reach Naveen and pulled back into playing alone.

qa.q: What small change did Naveen make on Saturday, and why might it help?
qa.a: He put the phone in a drawer and sat on the floor with Farhan. Short, fully present moments like this let Farhan see that his father is really there.

qa.q: How might Farhan's slow push of the car on Saturday look from Naveen's side?
qa.a: It may show Naveen that Farhan is willing to try again but is still checking whether he can be trusted.

grounding: A parent often absent in mind sees the child cry louder, then withdraw, and a short present moment begins repair.

passage:
"Papa! Papa!"
"One minute, Vidya, I'm on a call."
"PAPA!" A spoon clattered to the floor, then a cup.
"Vidya, no throwing." Pranav closed the laptop and sat down beside her. "You tapped my arm before and I did not turn. That was my miss. You are cross."
She sniffed. "Pa-pa. Look."
"Yes! Thank you for asking with words. I'm looking. What do you want to show me?"
She held up a wet sock.

qa.q: What did Vidya throw when she was not noticed?
qa.a: A spoon clattered to the floor, then a cup.

qa.q: Why did Vidya scream and throw things instead of waiting?
qa.a: She wanted her father's attention and had already been overlooked, so even an angry reaction was better than none.

qa.q: How did Pranav respond so that calm asking was rewarded and not only the storm?
qa.a: He set aside the laptop, named her feeling, owned that he had missed her tap, and thanked her for saying "Pa-pa. Look." 🙂

qa.q: How does Pranav's call look from Vidya's point of view?
qa.a: To her it is simply a time when Papa is not looking at her. She cannot yet wait or tell a call from being ignored.

grounding: A toddler tantrums for notice because angry attention beats none; the parent answers the need calmly and praises calm asking.

passage: The power went out in the village and thunder rolled over the fields. Hrishita woke screaming in the dark. Pankaj lifted her and rocked her by the door. "Main hoon. I am here. The rain will pass." His voice stayed low and slow. Hrishita's sobs turned into hiccups, then a thumb in her mouth. Weeks later, when a bucket clanged in the yard and she flinched, she patted her own chest and whispered, "Here, here," and looked for her father.

qa.q: Where did Pankaj rock Hrishita when the thunder came?
qa.a: He rocked her by the door after lifting her from the dark.

qa.q: What did Hrishita feel as her sobs turned into hiccups and a thumb in her mouth?
qa.a: She was calming down because she felt held and safe. The soft words and rocking showed her that someone was helping.

qa.q: Why is it useful that Pankaj says the same words each time?
qa.a: Repeating "I am here" teaches Hrishita that big feelings end and help comes. Over time she can begin to soothe herself, as her pat and "Here, here" hint. 🤍

qa.q: What might the clanging bucket show about how Hrishita sees her father now?
qa.a: She flinched but did not fall apart, and she still looked for Pankaj. This suggests her father is her safe place.

grounding: A rocking hold, a soft voice and the words 'I am here' teach the child that big feelings end and someone helps.

passage: Thomas, two, fell on the gravel outside the tea stall and scraped his palm. He sobbed and toddled straight past his mother's open arms to Dada Chinmay, who sat on the bench. Dada lifted him onto his lap and hummed the old lullaby. Thomas pressed his nose into Dada's shawl, sniffed its familiar smell, and his crying slowed. His mother smiled a little ruefully, then stroked Thomas's back too.

qa.q: Where did Thomas fall?
qa.a: He fell on the gravel outside the tea stall.

qa.q: Why did Thomas go past his mother to Dada Chinmay?
qa.a: He was hurt and wanted the lap, lullaby and smell he knows best. It shows a secure bond with his grandfather.

qa.q: How could Thomas's mother handle the moment so that everyone feels at ease?
qa.a: She can let Dada comfort him freely and add her own touch, as she did by stroking his back. Comfort from an elder does not mean she is replaced.

qa.q: What might Thomas's mother be thinking when she smiles "ruefully"?
qa.a: She may feel a small pang that he chose Dada, mixed with gladness that he is so loved and comforted. Her stroking shows she is not upset.

grounding: A hurt toddler seeks the lap, lullaby and smell of a familiar elder; it is healthy attachment and the parent need not feel replaced.

passage: Note for Chaitanya's parents, from Pradeep, his day carer. At your evening prayer, Chaitanya toddled over when you lit the lamp. He folded his hands, though the fingers did not quite meet, rang the bell twice and clapped when you sang. He giggled and kept peeking up at your faces. When he reached for the lamp I moved it higher and said, "Hot. We look." When he wandered off to his blocks, no one called him back, and I think that is right. 🙂

qa.q: How many times did Chaitanya ring the bell?
qa.a: He rang the bell twice.

qa.q: What seems to draw Chaitanya to the prayer, according to Pradeep?
qa.a: The note points to the lamp, the sounds and his family's faces. His giggling and peeking up suggest he is enjoying being with them, not feeling solemn belief.

qa.q: What did Pradeep do when Chaitanya reached for the lamp, and what else did the adults do well?
qa.a: Pradeep moved the lamp higher and said, "Hot. We look." The parents did not force him, and let him wander off to his blocks.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya's parents feel reading Pradeep's note?
qa.a: They may feel happy and reassured that he joins in warmly and that letting him leave was fine. It shows the ritual belongs to the family without pressure.

grounding: A toddler folds hands, rings the bell and claps because the family does; it is imitation and belonging, kept warm and unforced.
